questions.question: An object is placed 30 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Write the mirror formula substitution with correct signs, and say what a negative image distance means.
questions.solution: New Cartesian convention: distances measured from the pole, along incident light positive. u = −30 cm (object in front), f = −20 cm (concave mirror focus is on the same side as the object). 1/v + 1/u = 1/f → 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 + 1/30 = −1/60 → v = −60 cm. Negative v: the image is on the same side as the object — real, inverted, magnified m = −v/u = −2.

questions.concept: Why the mirror flips at f
questions.question: Move an object from just beyond a concave mirror's focus toward the mirror: describe the image's journey and identify the critical position.
questions.solution: Beyond C: real, inverted, diminished. At C: real, inverted, same size. Between C and F: real, inverted, magnified. AT F: image at infinity (reflected rays parallel). Inside F: virtual, erect, magnified (the shaving-mirror case). The focal point is the critical position where the image jumps from infinity (real side) to near infinity (virtual side).

questions.concept: Total internal reflection — the two conditions
questions.question: State the two conditions for total internal reflection, and explain why optical fibres need a dense core with a less dense cladding rather than bare glass in air.
questions.solution: Conditions: (1) light travels from the denser to the rarer medium; (2) angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle θc = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁). A fibre needs the cladding so total internal reflection happens at the CORE–CLADDING boundary with a well-defined critical angle; bare glass in air lets light leak at surface imperfections and contacts, and the cladding also protects the guiding surface.

questions.question: Light bends toward the normal entering glass. Explain the bending in terms of speed, and state what stays constant across the boundary.
questions.solution: Light slows in the denser medium (v = c/n); the wavefront pivots like a marching column stepping onto slower ground, bending toward the normal. Frequency stays constant (set by the source); wavelength shrinks to λ/n. Speed changes, frequency does not — the pair of answers the examiner checks.

questions.question: Using the lens maker's formula, explain why an air bubble in water behaves as a diverging lens even though glass lenses in air converge.
questions.solution: 1/f = (n₂/n₁ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂). Convergence depends on the RELATIVE refractive index n₂/n₁. Glass in air: ratio > 1 → converging (for convex). An air bubble in water: n₂/n₁ = 1.0/1.33 < 1, so the bracket flips sign — the same geometry now diverges. Convergence is a property of the pair of media, not the shape alone.

questions.question: Two thin lenses of powers +4 D and −2 D touch. Find the combined power and focal length, and state when the simple addition rule fails.
questions.solution: P = P₁ + P₂ = +2 D → f = 1/P = +0.5 m. The addition holds for thin lenses in CONTACT (or separated by much less than f). With a real separation d the equivalent power is P = P₁ + P₂ − d·P₁P₂ — the separation term is what the simple rule ignores.

questions.question: At minimum deviation through a prism, what is special about the ray's path inside, and why does the i–δ curve flatten there?
questions.solution: At minimum deviation the ray inside the prism is PARALLEL to the base — refraction at the two faces is symmetric (i = e, r₁ = r₂ = A/2). The deviation curve has zero slope there because δ decreases then increases; measuring the flat region gives the most accurate n via n = sin((A+δm)/2)/sin(A/2). Reading δ at a steep part of the curve amplifies error — that is why the minimum matters.

questions.question: Why does a simple microscope give the largest angular magnification when the final image is at the near point, yet the 'relaxed' setting is often preferred?
questions.solution: Image at the near point (D = 25 cm): M = 1 + D/f — largest because the angular size is maximal. Relaxed (image at infinity): M = D/f, slightly smaller but zero eye strain for prolonged use. The trade-off between maximum magnification and comfort is the expected discussion; both formulas must appear.
